title: The Jubilee of Hope (2025)
hookLine: a holy year of pilgrims of hope

lines: A CROWD ON THE LONG AVENUE.
A HOLY DOOR IN A PRISON.
cards: A crowd moves slowly down the long avenue toward Saint Peter's. Parish groups in matching shirts. Families pushing strollers.

An old man with a cane, keeping up. Across the city, inside a Roman prison, another group keeps the same holy year without leaving the building, because the pope came to them and opened a holy door there.
Both groups are pilgrims. Their year has a name and a motto: the Jubilee of Hope. Pilgrims of hope.

teach.b: Jubilee starts in the book of Leviticus, where the Hebrew word is yovel.
There God tells Israel to count off the years and then keep a special one: land goes back to the families who lost it, and people who had to sell themselves into service go free.
In the Douay-Rheims: "thou shalt sanctify the fiftieth year, and shalt proclaim remission to all the inhabitants of thy land: for it is the year of jubilee." Remission means release, a debt let go.

Tradition holds that the first Catholic holy year was declared in the Middle Ages, and since then popes have proclaimed them from time to time, with pilgrims receiving an indulgence, the Church's word for a release from the punishment still due for sins already forgiven.
Francis gave this jubilee its theme in a document called Spes non confundit, Latin for hope does not disappoint, a line of Saint Paul to the Romans, in the Douay-Rheims: "hope confoundeth not."
Paul gives the reason straight after: because the charity of God is poured forth in our hearts. A pilgrim isn't a tourist. A tourist goes to see something.

teach.h: A PILGRIM IS CHANGED ON THE WAY.
teach.b: A pilgrim goes to be changed on the way: the walking, the waiting, the sore feet, the prayer at the end.

teach.h: FOR IT IS THE YEAR OF JUBILEE.
teach.b: The jubilee asked Catholics to travel as pilgrims of hope, to Rome or to a church in their own diocese set aside for the year, and, in the old spirit of Leviticus, to let something go.
Partway through, the pope who opened it died; a new pope carried it on.

how: In a jubilee year, Catholics make pilgrimages to Rome or to churches their bishop designates, pass through holy doors, go to confession and receive Communion, and pray for the pope's intentions to receive the jubilee indulgence.

o: the Hebrew word for a year of release, behind jubilee
the Hebrew name for the holy door in Rome
a Hebrew blessing sung at the start of a pilgrimage

s: in Leviticus, the jubilee year is mainly a celebration
it is a year of release: land goes back to the families who lost it, and people in service go free.
the jubilee's theme comes from a line of Saint Paul
hope does not disappoint, from the letter to the Romans.
when the pope who opened the jubilee died, the holy year was called off

games.q: you're setting out on a pilgrimage. what makes it a pilgrimage and not a sightseeing trip?
o: going in order to be changed on the way.
getting there as fast as you can.
games.why: a tourist goes to see something; a pilgrim goes to be changed: the walking, the waiting, the prayer at the end.

practice: A pilgrimage doesn't need a plane: picture a walk to a place nearby that means something, a church, a cemetery, a bench where someone you loved used to sit.
Decide what you'd carry on the way, a hope or a worry, and what you'd set down when you arrive. If you pray, pray as you walk; if you don't, let the walking itself be the attention.

wordCard.voice: Yovel, the Hebrew word behind jubilee. A holy year opened by Francis, built on Paul's line that hope does not disappoint, with the motto pilgrims of hope.

orig.note: Hebrew: jubilee, the year of release in Leviticus 25.

carryVoice: Your line: pilgrims of hope. Hope, Paul says, does not disappoint. That's day nine hundred forty-one.
